facts.text: The tardigrade (water bear) can survive being cooled to -272°C (just one degree above absolute zero) and heated to 150°C, withstand pressure six times greater than the deepest ocean trenches, and has survived direct exposure to the vacuum of space for at least 10 days in orbital experiments.
facts.verification_note: Tardigrades have been documented in peer-reviewed studies to survive temperatures from near absolute zero (-272°C) to 150°C, pressures exceeding 600 MPa (roughly 6x deeper than ocean trenches), and direct space exposure for 10+ days during the FOTON-M3 mission in 2007.
facts.image_description: A photorealistic tardigrade floats at the center of a triptych composition, its translucent, segmented body rendered in pale amber and cream tones with eight stubby legs extended. The background splits into three dramatic environments: the left shows a deep blue-black cryogenic frost with crystalline ice formations at -272°C, the center depicts the inky void of space with distant stars and the curved edge of Earth below, and the right glows with intense orange-red heat waves at 150°C. Dramatic lighting emanates from each environment—cold blue luminescence from the left, stark white starlight from above, and fierce amber glow from the right—all converging on the tardigrade's semi-transparent body to reveal its internal structures, while depth-of-field effects keep the creature in sharp focus against the extreme conditions surrounding it.

facts.text: Bananas are naturally radioactive due to their high potassium-40 content, and eating one exposes you to approximately 0.1 microsieverts of radiation—about 1% of your daily background radiation dose.
facts.verification_note: Bananas contain potassium-40, a naturally occurring radioactive isotope, and do expose consumers to approximately 0.1 microsieverts of radiation, which is roughly 1% of typical daily background radiation exposure of 10 microsieverts.
facts.image_description: A split-screen scientific illustration showing a photorealistic yellow banana on the left side with a soft glow emanating from within, rendered with subtle green sparkles representing potassium-40 atoms dispersed throughout its flesh. The right side displays a transparent cross-section of the banana with glowing purple and blue particles visualizing radiation emissions as delicate, wispy trails, while a small digital meter overlay shows "0.1 μSv" in crisp white numbers. The background transitions from warm cream to cool gray-blue, with a subtle comparison scale showing the banana's radiation as a tiny highlighted segment of a larger bar representing daily background radiation exposure. The style blends clean technical diagram aesthetics with a touch of ethereal beauty, using soft lighting that makes the radioactive elements appear magical rather than menacing.

facts.text: The mantis shrimp can punch with an acceleration of over 10,000 times the force of gravity, moving so fast that it boils the water around its strike and creates bursts of light called sonoluminescence through the resulting cavitation bubbles.
facts.verification_note: Mantis shrimp strikes do reach accelerations exceeding 10,000 g, create cavitation bubbles that collapse to produce localized heating and sonoluminescence, though the water doesn't technically "boil" in the conventional sense but rather undergoes cavitation.
facts.image_description: The illustration depicts a vibrant peacock mantis shrimp in mid-strike against a deep ocean blue background, its raptorial appendage extended in a blur of motion toward a crab shell. The focal point is the explosive moment of impact, where the water erupts in a spectacular display of translucent cavitation bubbles rendered in ethereal whites and silvers, with pinpoints of electric blue and green bioluminescent light bursting from within them—the sonoluminescence effect. The style blends photorealistic detail of the mantis shrimp's iridescent greens, oranges, and blues with a scientific cross-section overlay showing the physics at work: motion lines indicating the incredible speed, small text annotations marking "10,400g acceleration," and a thermal gradient visualization showing the localized heating of water molecules in reds and yellows around the strike zone. The composition uses dramatic lighting with the glowing cavitation bubbles creating a halo effect that draws the eye to the center of the action, while the mantis shrimp's compound eyes gleam with predatory focus in the foreground.

facts.text: The Eiffel Tower grows approximately 15 centimeters taller during summer due to thermal expansion of its iron structure when heated by the sun, then contracts back to its original height in winter.
facts.verification_note: The Eiffel Tower's iron structure does expand by approximately 15 centimeters during summer heat due to thermal expansion, with the metal expanding as temperatures rise and contracting as they fall.
facts.image_description: A split-panel scientific illustration showing the Eiffel Tower in contrasting seasons: the left panel depicts winter with the tower in cool steel-blue tones under pale gray skies, with a subtle measurement line indicating its baseline height; the right panel shows summer with the same tower bathed in warm golden sunlight and orange-amber hues, with a clearly marked measurement line 15 centimeters higher and subtle upward arrows along the iron lattice structure to indicate expansion. The iron beams should have a slight visual shimmer or heat-wave distortion in the summer panel, with thermometer graphics overlaid showing temperature differences, while maintaining a clean, educational infographic style with precise measurement annotations and a color-coded legend explaining thermal expansion. Small molecular diagrams of iron atoms spreading apart could float near the structure's joints, making the invisible process of thermal expansion visible and scientifically accurate.

facts.text: Honey never spoils due to its low water content and acidic pH, and archaeologists have found 3,000-year-old honey in Egyptian tombs that was still perfectly edible.
facts.verification_note: Honey's low water activity (around 0.6), acidic pH (3.2-4.5), and production of hydrogen peroxide create an inhospitable environment for microbial growth, and archaeologists have indeed discovered ancient honey in Egyptian tombs that remained preserved, though "perfectly edible" is somewhat subjective regarding palatability versus safety.
facts.image_description: The illustration should depict a split scene in warm, golden-amber tones: on the left, an ancient Egyptian tomb interior with hieroglyphic-covered stone walls illuminated by torch light, showing a clay honey jar among dusty treasures, with a translucent cross-section revealing pristine, glowing honey inside. On the right, a modern laboratory setting in cool blues and whites shows the same honey being examined under scientific equipment, with floating diagrams indicating pH levels (3.9) and water content percentages (<20%), connected by a flowing ribbon of liquid gold that bridges the 3,000-year gap. The style should blend photorealistic elements with scientific infographic details, using dramatic chiaroscuro lighting to emphasize the honey's eternal, jewel-like quality, while microscopic hexagonal crystalline structures and water molecules float around the ancient jar to visualize the scientific principles at work.
